item.title: The Republican Strategy to Salvage the Midterms
item.description:
With Republicans trailing in the polls, the party is making hard choices about where to spend its money — abandoning some races while pouring resources into others.

Shane Goldmacher, Nate Cohn and Lisa Lerer, political correspondents for The New York Times, explain why President Trump is campaigning almost daily in deep-red territory, how his influence is shaping the strategy and whether Democrats can win over the disenchanted voters they may need to take back the House and the Senate.

Guests: 

  • Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.
  • Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.
  • Lisa Lerer, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Economic pain and an unpopular Trump have put the G.O.P. on its heels.
  • Top Republican groups are pulling support from two House incumbents.

Photo: Kenny Holston/The New York Times

item.title: The U.S. Tried to Choke Russia’s Energy Market. Then It Made a Diesel Deal.
item.description:
President Trump announced a deal to purchase Russian diesel fuel and temporarily suspended sanctions in an effort to lower domestic fuel prices amid rising costs from the war in Iran and in anticipation of the upcoming midterms. This abrupt foreign policy shift stunned European allies and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine, which viewed the move as a weakening of Western leverage against Russia.

Today, Anton Troianovski, a global affairs correspondent for The New York Times, discusses what the deal reveals about the Trump administration’s strategy with Russia, and how much it could actually lower prices at the pump.

Guest: Anton Troianovski, a global affairs correspondent for The New York Times who writes about foreign policy, national security and America’s place in the world.

Background reading: Trump faces a new crisis over Ukraine following the Russian diesel deal.

Photo: Igor Grussak/picture alliance via Getty Images

item.title: When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to helping solve some of mathematics’ most famous open problems — and the field is reckoning with what that means.

Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University, describes the excitement and grief of watching A.I. take on work that gives people a sense of purpose — and asks what could be lost if machines deliver answers without the human struggle, insight and understanding that make solving problems meaningful.

Guest: Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University who writes for The New York Times about the future of research.

Background reading: 

  • Mathematics isn’t just a game to let A.I. solve — history shows why.
  • A.I. is mastering the kinds of projects that have long helped to build the careers of young mathematicians. What does that mean for their future?
  • Steven Strogatz’s forthcoming book: Big Math.

Photo: Ian C. Bates for The New York Times

item.title: The Israeli Film Directors Pushing for a Reckoning in Their Home Country
item.description:
The documentary film “NAZA,” which investigates the methods the Israeli military has used in the war in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, received a record-breaking standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival last month. Just a few days later, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would propose legislation that could revoke the directors’ Israeli citizenship, arguing that they had defamed their country.

Now, with a global theatrical release underway, the directors spoke with “The Daily” to discuss the film and all the pushback that it — and they — have experienced.

Guest: 

  • Rachel Szor, an Israeli investigative journalist, film director and activist.
  • Yuval Abraham, an Israeli investigative journalist, film director and Arabic-Hebrew translator.

Background reading: 

  • After accolades abroad, “NAZA” met backlash at home.
  • Read The Times’s review of the film.

Photo: Stefano Rellandini/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, The Guardian/IFC Center, Ander Gillenea/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: Celine Dion’s Triumphant Return to the Stage
item.description:
A dramatic pop music comeback story is underway: Celine Dion is performing again.

In 2022, Dion, the renowned Canadian singer, announced that she had stiff person syndrome, a rare and incurable neurological disorder that causes painful muscle spasms and affects roughly one in a million people. The announcement came as a shock to her fans, and in a raw and revealing documentary released in 2024, “I Am: Celine Dion," she shared her struggle to overcome her condition, and sing again. But Dion worked her way back to performing, and is now appearing in a run of sold out shows in Paris.

The culture reporter Elisabeth Vincentelli was there on opening night, and in this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” she talks with our host Natalie Kitroeff about the remarkable comeback of Celine Dion.

On Today’s Episode:

  • Elisabeth Vincentelli, an arts, culture, and theater journalist.

Background Reading:

  • Celine Dion Is Back Onstage. Naturally, She Chose Paris.
  • Paris Really, Really Loves Celine Dion

Photo credit: Clementine Schneidermann for The New York Times.

item.title: Why France Is in Crisis
item.description:
For weeks, thousands of high school students in France have been out in the streets protesting the conditions of public schools. They want better funding, something that won’t be easy with the current state of French finances.

Mark Landler, the Paris bureau chief, explains why after years of overspending, France is in crisis, and is driving toward a fiscal cliff.

Guest: Mark Landler, the Paris bureau chief of The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • France’s debt problem is a warning to the world.
  • Understand the country’s polycrisis.
  • For the resurgent far left, the protests are an opening and a threat.

Photo: Miguel Medina/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: A Failed Execution and the Future of the Death Penalty
item.description:
Christa Pike survived two doses of a lethal injection drug last week during a botched execution in Tennessee.

Pamela Colloff, who writes for The New York Times Magazine, discusses the waning public support for the death penalty and why despite it some states are doubling down.

Guest: Pamela Colloff, a reporter at ProPublica and a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine.

item.title: Three Vans, a Startled Farmer and an Iranian Plot Against the U.S.
item.description:
What exactly happened near an air base in Britain used by the United States?

Eric Schmitt, a national security correspondent for The New York Times, discusses what he’s learned about the mysterious events around the base, including the abrupt withdrawal of U.S. Air Force bombers.

Guest: Eric Schmitt, a national security correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • A mysterious call near a military base used by the United States set in motion a huge counterterrorism response and days of uncertainty in Britain.
  • The United States withdrew 12 bombers from the base after information emerged about a potential Iranian drone attack, U.S. and British officials said.

item.title: Midterm Surprise: Democrats Are Surging in Red America
item.description:
A new set of polls from The New York Times finds that Democratic candidates are doing remarkably well in the Republican-leaning states that they need to win to gain control of the U.S. Senate in next month’s midterm elections.

They are doing less well in the blue states that, in theory, should be easier to win.

Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The Times, offers his idea of what is behind the numbers.

Guest: Nate Cohn, The New York Times’s chief political analyst.

Background reading: 

  • Polls suggested that Hispanic voters, whose support helped propel President Trump to the White House in 2024, would largely support the Democratic Party this time.
  • Senator Susan Collins of Maine led polls for the first time since Graham Platner dropped out of the race in July.

item.title: The Restaurant Industry Is Broken. Can It Be Fixed?
item.description:
If you dine out regularly, you might have noticed some changes in restaurants over the past few years. Perhaps you’ve found yourself ordering at a counter, scanning a QR code to see the menu, or eating … a lot more soft serve.

These changes aren’t just trends. Brett Anderson, a New York Times food reporter, says they are restaurant owners’ desperate attempts to stay afloat in an industry in crisis. According to a report from the National Restaurant Association, 42 percent of restaurant owners said they weren’t profitable in 2025. Many of them were at serious risk of closing.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Brett talks with our host Michael Barbaro about the economic realities that are forcing businesses to rethink the entire concept of a restaurant, including a radical experiment at one Minneapolis diner that stopped charging for food entirely.

On Today’s Episode:

  • Brett Anderson, a reporter for the Food section of The New York Times.

Background Reading:

  • This Restaurant Stopped Charging for Food. And Profits Are Up.

  • The Restaurant List 2026

item.title: Inside the Devastating Hack of the F.B.I.
item.description:
A little over a decade ago, after hackers broke into the U.S. government and stole the personnel records of millions of federal workers, officials vowed that it would never happen again. Something similar recently did — to the F.B.I.

item.title: He Was Deported to a Country He’d Never Heard Of
item.description:
In its efforts to deport as many undocumented immigrants as possible, the Trump administration has increasingly relied on a highly controversial strategy: deporting people to countries they have no connection to.

Last week, a federal court ruled the practice to be illegal because it violated people’s right to due process. The administration challenged that ruling, and now it is in front of the Supreme Court.

Nicholas Casey tells the story of Roberto Mosquera, who moved to the United States from Cuba as a child. He has been held in the small country of Eswatini since July 2025.

Guest: Nicholas Casey, a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine who writes about geopolitics.

Background reading: 

  • He was deported to a country he’d never heard of. He may never go free.
  • How do you interview a deportee being held inside a maximum-security prison?

item.title: The Best TV Shows of the 21st Century
item.description:
The turn of the century was the beginning of a new era in television: prestige TV for the masses. Today, television is where big stars and innovative creators go to marshal sizable budgets and tell meaningful stories.

Over recent months, our colleagues at The New York Times ran a survey, asking industry insiders — on-screen talent, writers, directors, producers, executives and others — to pick their top 10 television series of the last 26 years. We compiled their responses into a list, published this week, of the best TV of the 21st century.

In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” The Times’s canon editor, Gilbert Cruz, and our chief TV critic, James Poniewozik, talk with our host Natalie Kitroeff about what made the list, and what didn’t.

 

On Today’s Episode

James Poniewozik is The New York Times’s chief TV critic.

Gilbert Cruz is the canon editor at The New York Times.

 

Background Reading

  • The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century
  • The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: Cast Your Vote
  • The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: How Stars, Creators and Other TV Lovers Voted
